claim: The CMG helicase separates DNA strands during replication in eukaryotes.
source: The Cdc45/Mcm2-7/GINS (CMG) helicase separates DNA strands during replication in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a fundamental statement about CMG function presented in the abstract, supported by the broader scientific literature on eukaryotic DNA replication.

claim: The structure of the CMG was determined in the presence of ATPγS and a DNA duplex bearing a 3′ single-stranded tail using electron microscopy.
source: Using electron microscopy, we have determined the structure of the CMG in the presence of ATPγS and a DNA duplex bearing a 3′ single-stranded tail.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used to determine the structure, which is supported by the methods section and EM data presented.

claim: The MCM subunits of the CMG bind preferentially to single-stranded DNA.
source: The structure shows that the MCM subunits of the CMG bind preferentially to single-stranded DNA
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data and biochemical observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structure establishes the polarity by which DNA enters into the Mcm2-7 pore.
source: The structure shows that the MCM subunits of the CMG bind preferentially to single-stranded DNA, establishes the polarity by which DNA enters into the Mcm2-7 pore
evidence: The structural data showing DNA orientation relative to the CMG complex provides direct evidence for DNA entry polarity.

claim: Cdc45 helps prevent DNA from dissociating from the helicase.
source: establishes the polarity by which DNA enters into the Mcm2-7 pore, and explains how Cdc45 helps prevent DNA from dissociating from the helicase.
evidence: The structural positioning of Cdc45 and its RecJ domain orientation provide evidence for this function.

claim: The Mcm2-7 subcomplex forms a cracked-ring, right-handed spiral when DNA and nucleotide are bound.
source: The Mcm2-7 subcomplex forms a cracked-ring, right-handed spiral when DNA and nucleotide are bound
evidence: The EM structure directly shows this spiral configuration in the presence of DNA and ATPγS.

claim: The CMG exhibits unexpected congruencies with bacterial DnaB helicases.
source: The Mcm2-7 subcomplex forms a cracked-ring, right-handed spiral when DNA and nucleotide are bound, revealing unexpected congruencies between the CMG and both bacterial DnaB helicases and the AAA+ motor of the eukaryotic proteasome.
evidence: Structural comparison between CMG and DnaB reveals similar spiral architectures and channel dimensions.

claim: The CMG exhibits unexpected congruencies with the AAA+ motor of the eukaryotic proteasome.
source: The Mcm2-7 subcomplex forms a cracked-ring, right-handed spiral when DNA and nucleotide are bound, revealing unexpected congruencies between the CMG and both bacterial DnaB helicases and the AAA+ motor of the eukaryotic proteasome.
evidence: Structural comparison shows similar organization of AAA+ domains and accessory subunit positioning between CMG and proteasome.

claim: A subpopulation of dimeric CMGs exists.
source: The existence of a subpopulation of dimeric CMGs establishes the subunit register of Mcm2-7 double hexamers
evidence: EM data shows approximately 5% of CMG particles form dimers with a defined head-to-head configuration.

claim: The dimeric CMG structure establishes the subunit register of Mcm2-7 double hexamers.
source: The existence of a subpopulation of dimeric CMGs establishes the subunit register of Mcm2-7 double hexamers
evidence: Analysis of 2D class averages of CMG dimers compared to computational models reveals the specific subunit arrangement.

claim: Mcm2-7 transitions through different conformational and assembly states as it matures into a functional helicase.
source: together with the spiral form highlights how Mcm2-7 transitions through different conformational and assembly states as it matures into a functional helicase.
evidence: Comparison of different structural states (apo, nucleotide-bound, DNA-bound, dimeric) reveals conformational changes.

claim: Mcm2-7 is a ring-shaped helicase that serves as the principal unwinding activity for separating parental DNA strands in eukaryotes.
source: In eukaryotes, origins are licensed for replication by recruitment of the Mcm2-7 complex, a ring-shaped helicase that serves as the principal unwinding activity for separating parental DNA strands (Blow, 1993; Bochman and Schwacha, 2008; Costa et al., 2011; Lyubimov et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work establishing Mcm2-7 function.

claim: Mcm2-7 is initially loaded around duplex DNA as an inactive double hexamer by ORC, Cdc6, and Cdt1 in the G1 phase of the cell cycle.
source: Mcm2-7 is initially loaded around duplex DNA as an inactive double hexamer by the origin recognition complex (ORC), Cdc6, and Cdt1 in the G1 phase of the cell cycle (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by cited biochemical studies showing Mcm2-7 loading mechanism.

claim: The Mcm2-7 double hexamer forms a stable intermediate known as the pre-replicative complex (pre-RC).
source: forming a stable intermediate known as the pre-replicative complex (pre-RC, Diffley et al., 1994; Donovan et al., 1997; Maiorano et al., 2000; Sun et al., 2013; Yanagi et al., 2002).
evidence: Multiple citations support the characterization of the pre-RC as a stable intermediate.

claim: Upon entry into S phase, Mcm2-7 associates with the GINS complex and Cdc45 generating an 11-member assembly termed the CMG.
source: Upon entry into S phase, Mcm2-7 associates with the GINS complex and Cdc45 generating an 11-member assembly termed the CMG (Kanemaki et al., 2003; Gambus et al., 2006; Moyer et al., 2006; Pacek et al., 2006; Ilves et al., 2010).
evidence: Multiple citations document the formation of the CMG complex during S phase.

claim: GINS/Cdc45 assembly is dependent on the CDK kinase.
source: GINS/Cdc45 assembly is dependent on the CDK kinase (Zegerman and Diffley, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on CDK-dependent CMG assembly.

claim: Post-translational modification of Mcm subunits 2, 4, and 6 by the Cdc7/Dbf4 kinase (DDK) contributes to CMG activation.
source: while post-translational modification of Mcm subunits 2, 4, and 6 by the Cdc7/Dbf4 kinase (DDK) further contributes to CMG activation (Labib, 2010; Sheu and Stillman, 2010).
evidence: Citations support the role of DDK phosphorylation in CMG activation.

claim: The two CMG particles split apart into discrete complexes that have been proposed to each encircle a single DNA strand during translocation.
source: Following the assembly of replicative polymerases and replisomal scaffolding factors (Gambus et al., 2009; Muramatsu et al., 2010), the two CMG particles split apart into discrete complexes that have been proposed to each encircle a single DNA strand during translocation (Yardimci et al., 2010; Boos et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations to prior work support the model of CMG separation and single-strand encirclement.

claim: The precise register by which Mcm2-7 subunits interact with each other across the two rings in a double-hexamer is not known.
source: Although the six homologous subunits of one Mcm2-7 complex are known to pair with a second Mcm2-7 complex through their N-terminal domains in the context of a double-hexamer (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009), the precise register by which these subunits interact with each other across the two rings is not known.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: DDK phosphorylates the N-termini of Mcm2, Mcm6, and Mcm4.
source: How DDK phosphorylation of the Mcm2, Mcm6, and Mcm4 N-termini (Labib, 2010)
evidence: Citation supports the identification of DDK phosphorylation targets.

claim: A DDK-bypass mutation exists in the N-terminus of Mcm4.
source: or how a DDK-bypass mutation in the N-terminus of either Mcm4 (Sheu and Stillman, 2010)
evidence: Citation documents the existence of a DDK-bypass mutation in Mcm4.

claim: A DDK-bypass mutation exists in the N-terminus of Mcm5.
source: or Mcm5 (Jackson et al., 1993)
evidence: Citation documents the existence of a DDK-bypass mutation in Mcm5.

claim: Mcm4 is spatially segregated from Mcm2 and Mcm5 in the CMG structure.
source: particularly as Mcm4 is spatially segregated from Mcm2 and Mcm5 (Costa et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to prior structural work establishes the spatial arrangement of Mcm subunits.

claim: The CMG translocates 3′→5′ along DNA during unwinding and fork progression.
source: During unwinding and fork progression, the CMG translocates 3′→5′ along DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CMG directionality supported by prior biochemical studies.

claim: Cdc45 contains a RecJ exonuclease domain that can bind DNA but is catalytically inactive.
source: Cdc45 has recently been shown to contain a RecJ exonuclease domain that can bind DNA but that is catalytically inactive (Petojevic et al., unpublished data, as well as Sanchez-Pulido and Ponting, 2011; Krastanova et al., 2012; Szambowska et al., 2014).
evidence: Multiple citations and unpublished data support the identification and characterization of the Cdc45 RecJ domain.

claim: Conflicting models exist for how Mcm2-7 engages substrate DNAs as it moves 3′→5′ during strand separation.
source: Conflicting models likewise exist for how Mcm2-7 engages substrate DNAs as it moves 3′→5′ during strand separation, with biochemical data from archaeal MCMs and phylogenetic relationships to superfamily III (SFIII) helicases (such as the SV40 Large T antigen and the papillomavirus E1 protein) predicting mutually exclusive binding orientations (McGeoch et al., 2005; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Rothenberg et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Citations to prior work document conflicting models for MCM DNA engagement.

claim: The structure was determined using Drosophila melanogaster CMG.
source: To begin to understand several extant questions surrounding how the CMG is formed and operates at molecular level, we have determined structure of the full-length complex from Drosophila melanogaster
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the organism source of the CMG complex.

claim: The structure was determined in the presence of a 3′-tailed DNA duplex and ATPγS using negative-stain electron microscopy and single-particle reconstruction methods.
source: we have determined structure of the full-length complex from Drosophila melanogaster in the presence of a 3′-tailed DNA duplex and the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog, ATPγS, using negative-stain electron microscopy and single-particle reconstruction methods.
evidence: The methods used for structure determination are explicitly described.

claim: The C-terminal ATPase domains of Mcm2-7 form the leading edge of the motor as it advances on a duplex.
source: The structure establishes that: 1) the CMG preferentially associates with single-stranded DNAs over double-stranded substrates, 2) the C-terminal ATPase domains of Mcm2-7 form the leading edge of the motor as it advances on a duplex
evidence: The structural data showing DNA orientation relative to the CMG establishes this polarity.

claim: The RecJ domain of Cdc45 is oriented to favor the capture of DNA segments that might accidentally escape the Mcm2-7 pore.
source: and 3) the RecJ domain of Cdc45 is oriented to favor the capture of DNA segments that might accidently escape the Mcm2-7 pore.
evidence: The structural positioning of the Cdc45 RecJ domain relative to the Mcm2/5 gate supports this functional interpretation.

claim: The Mcm2-7 ATPase domains transition from a planar, open ring to a closed, right-handed spiral in the presence of both DNA and nucleotide.
source: Comparison of the new structure with a previously-determined apo CMG model (Costa et al., 2011) shows that the Mcm2-7 ATPase domains of the complex transition from a planar, open ring into a closed, right-handed spiral in the presence of both DNA and nucleotide.
evidence: Comparison between apo and DNA/nucleotide-bound structures reveals this conformational change.

claim: The MCM spiral is most similar to that adopted by the bacterial DnaB helicase upon engaging single-stranded DNA.
source: Analysis of this state alongside other ring-ATPases shows that the MCM spiral is most similar to that adopted by the bacterial DnaB helicase upon engaging single-stranded DNA (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012)
evidence: Structural comparison with DnaB structure supports this similarity.

claim: GINS•Cdc45 bridges the junction between the ends of the spiral in a manner similar to how Rpn1 spans a spiral Rpt1-6 ATPase assembly in the eukaryotic proteasome.
source: and that the GINS•Cdc45 complex bridges the junction between the ends of the spiral in a manner similar to that by which the Rpn1 accessory subunit spans a spiral Rpt1-6 ATPase assembly in the eukaryotic proteasome (Lander et al., 2012).
evidence: Structural comparison with proteasome structure reveals this architectural similarity.

claim: Examination of CMG dimers shows how two Mcm2-7 complexes associate within a double hexamer.
source: Interestingly, examination of a subpopulation of CMG dimers present in our EM data shows how two Mcm2-7 complexes associate within a double hexamer
evidence: Analysis of dimeric CMG particles in the EM data reveals the double hexamer organization.

claim: The dimerized CMG state persists during CMG formation, prior to separation during fork progression.
source: and suggests that this dimerized state persists during CMG formation, prior to separation during fork progression (Ilves et al., 2010; Yardimci et al., 2010).
evidence: The observation of CMG dimers combined with cited work on CMG separation supports this model.

claim: Mcm2-7 unwinds DNA using an approach distinct from that of superfamily III helicases.
source: Collectively, our observations establish that Mcm2-7 unwinds DNA using an approach distinct from that of superfamily III helicases
evidence: The opposite DNA polarity observed compared to SF3 helicases supports this conclusion.

claim: A previous study determined medium-resolution (28 Å) structures of the Drosophila melanogaster CMG helicase in both an apo state and bound to a non-hydrolyzable ATP analog.
source: In a previous study, we determined the medium-resolution (28 Å) structures of the Drosophila melanogaster CMG helicase in both an apo state and bound to a non-hydrolyzable ATP analog (Costa et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to prior work by the authors documents these previous structures.

claim: Previous CMG models revealed a planar structure for Mcm2-7, with GINS and Cdc45 spanning a gap between Mcm2 and Mcm5 when nucleotide was omitted.
source: Though sufficient for mapping individual subunits within the CMG, both models revealed a planar structure for Mcm2-7, with GINS and Cdc45 spanning a gap that appeared between Mcm2 and Mcm5 when nucleotide was omitted.
evidence: Description of prior structural findings from cited work.

claim: A total of 29,913 particles were selected from EM micrographs for the current study.
source: A total of 29,913 particles were selected from EM micrographs acquired with JADAS automated data collection software (JEOL, Zhang et al., 2009) on a JEM2100 electron microscope.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of particles used in the analysis.

claim: The current CMG structure was determined to 18 Å resolution.
source: CMG particles imaged with DNA and ATPγS turned out to be quite uniform, permitting structure determination to a higher resolution than that obtained previously (18 Å vs 28 Å resolution, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The resolution is explicitly stated and supported by FSC analysis shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The location of Psf1 C-terminus was not visible in previous structures but is clearly evident in the new structure.
source: For instance, the location of Psf1 C-terminus, which was previously not visible, was now clearly evident, and could be readily fit to a recently-published full-length structure of Psf1 from an archaeal ortholog (Oyama et al., 2011; Figure 1C).
evidence: The improved resolution allows visualization of previously unseen structural features, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Flexing within the Mcm2-7 ring is apparent with the C-terminal lobes of different MCM subunits displaying markedly distinct degrees of movement with respect to their associated N-terminal regions.
source: Flexing within the Mcm2-7 ring was also apparent with the C-terminal lobes of different MCM subunits displaying markedly distinct degrees of movement with respect to their associated N-terminal regions (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The structural data shown in Figure 1D,E demonstrates differential positioning of MCM domains.

claim: Asymmetric positioning between the two tiers of an MCM ring has not been reported previously.
source: Asymmetric positioning between the two tiers of an MCM ring has not been reported previously
evidence: This identifies a novel structural observation from the current study.

claim: The N-terminal and C-terminal domains of MCM are conformationally independent of each other to some extent in the presence of DNA substrates.
source: demonstrating that these elements are conformationally independent of each other to some extent in the presence of DNA substrates.
evidence: The observed differential flexing between N- and C-terminal domains supports this conclusion.

claim: A rod-shaped feature jutting away from the C-terminal face of Mcm subunits 2 and 5 is present in electron density maps of the DNA-bound CMG.
source: More concrete evidence for DNA association was apparent in electron density maps generated for the CMG, which showed a rod-shaped feature jutting away from the C-terminal face of Mcm subunits 2 and 5 (Figure 2A)
evidence: The electron density map shown in Figure 2A directly shows this feature.

claim: The rod-shaped feature is absent in DNA-free 3D reconstructions of the CMG.
source: this feature is absent in DNA-free 3D reconstructions of the CMG (Costa et al., 2011).
evidence: Comparison with prior DNA-free structures shows this feature is specific to DNA-bound state.

claim: Biotin-labeling of the duplex end of the oligonucleotide followed by streptavidin binding shows additional density in 2D class averages compared to unlabeled CMG–DNA particles.
source: Inspection of the resultant 2D class averages from this approach revealed clear additional density compared to the unlabeled CMG–DNA particles (Figure 2B), demonstrating that the tailed substrate indeed associates with the complex particles.
evidence: The 2D class averages shown in Figure 2B provide direct visual evidence of streptavidin labeling.

claim: The CMG binds to the single-stranded end of the 3′-tailed DNA substrate.
source: Given the electron density features seen for the DNA and the distance the streptavidin 'pointer' resides from the complex, the EM data show that the CMG binds to the single-stranded end of the 3′-tailed DNA substrate
evidence: The position of streptavidin relative to the CMG in the EM data supports this conclusion.

claim: The CMG preferentially associates with and translocates along single-stranded DNA over duplex substrates.
source: corroborating biochemical data indicating that the complex preferentially associates with and translocates along single-stranded DNA over duplex substrates (Ilves et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2011).
evidence: Citations to prior biochemical studies support this preference for ssDNA.

claim: In E1, the 3′ end of DNA has been observed by X-ray crystallography to lie proximal to the C-terminal motor domains of the helicase.
source: In E1, the 3′ end of DNA has been observed by X-ray crystallography to lie proximal to the C-terminal motor domains of the helicase (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006).
evidence: Citation to prior structural work on E1 helicase.

claim: Based on FRET measurements, the converse DNA orientation has been reported for Sulfolobus solfataricus MCM compared to E1.
source: By contrast, based on FRET measurements between a dye-labeled DNA/MCM pair, the converse has been reported for Sulfolobus solfataricus MCM (McGeoch et al., 2005; Rothenberg et al., 2007).
evidence: Citations to prior FRET studies on archaeal MCM.

claim: The streptavidin appended to the duplex DNA end localizes next to the C-terminal, AAA+ domain face of the CMG particle.
source: In the new CMG structure, the streptavidin appended to the duplex DNA end can be clearly seen to localize next to the C-terminal, AAA+ domain face of the particle (Figure 2B).
evidence: Figure 2B shows the position of streptavidin relative to the CMG structure.

claim: A DNA segment bound by an MCM runs from the N-terminal collar to the ATPase motor region in a 3′ to 5′ direction.
source: This finding not only demonstrates that a DNA segment bound by an MCM runs from the N-terminal collar to the ATPase motor region in a 3′ to 5′ direction
evidence: The streptavidin labeling experiment establishes the DNA polarity through the MCM pore.

claim: MCM and SF3 helicases bind substrates with opposing polarities.
source: but also indicates that MCM and SF3 helicases bind substrates with opposing polarities.
evidence: Comparison of DNA orientation in CMG versus E1 structures reveals opposite polarities.

claim: The N-terminus of Cdc45 belongs to the RecJ family of ssDNA exonucleases.
source: Recently, however, the N-terminus of Cdc45 was shown to belong to the RecJ family of ssDNA exonucleases (Sanchez-Pulido and Ponting, 2011).
evidence: Citation to prior work identifying the RecJ domain in Cdc45.

claim: Within the RecJ family, Cdc45 belongs to an offshoot branch that can still bind DNA but possesses natural amino acid substitutions which inactivate hydrolase functions.
source: Interestingly, within this grouping, Cdc45 belongs to an offshoot branch that can still bind DNA, but that also possesses natural amino acid substitutions which would appear to inactivate any native hydrolase functions (Krastanova et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation to prior work characterizing the inactive exonuclease domain of Cdc45.

claim: A homology model for DmCdc45 was built based on Thermus thermophilus RecJ.
source: To understand how the RecJ fold of Cdc45 interfaces with Mcm2-7 and GINS, we built a homology model for DmCdc45 based on Thermus thermophilus RecJ and docked it into the higher-resolution, DNA-bound CMG reconstruction.
evidence: The methods describe the homology modeling approach used.

claim: The catalytic core and DNA tracking domain of the Cdc45 homology model fit unambiguously into only one region of the Cdc45 density.
source: The catalytic core and DNA tracking domain of the homology model fit unambiguously into only one region of the Cdc45 density (Figure 3A)
evidence: Figure 3A shows the docking of the RecJ homology model into the EM density.

claim: The Cdc45 RecJ domain appears to contact the C-terminal 'B-domain' of Psf1.
source: Notably, in placing the Cdc45 RecJ domain, we found that this element appeared to contact the now-apparent C-terminal 'B-domain' of Psf1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The structural model shown in Figure 3A suggests this interaction.

claim: Ablation of the Psf1 B-domain region (residues 185–202) prevented CMG formation under the conditions used to purify the intact assembly.
source: Ablation of either the Psf1 B-domain region (residues 185–202) or Cdc45 N-terminal region (residues 1–99) prevented CMG formation under the conditions used to purify the intact assembly (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 demonstrate the requirement for these regions.

claim: Ablation of the Cdc45 N-terminal region (residues 1–99) prevented CMG formation under the conditions used to purify the intact assembly.
source: Ablation of either the Psf1 B-domain region (residues 185–202) or Cdc45 N-terminal region (residues 1–99) prevented CMG formation under the conditions used to purify the intact assembly (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 demonstrate the requirement for these regions.

claim: A quadruple Psf1 mutant (E190A/L192A/V193A/R194A) was unable to interact with Cdc45.
source: Likewise, while point mutations were unable to disrupt CMG formation as judged by co-immunoprecipitation, a quadruple Psf1 mutant (E190A/L192A/V193A/R194A) proved unable to interact with Cdc45.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate loss of Cdc45 interaction with this mutant.

claim: The Cdc45–Psf1 interaction plays a critical role in CMG formation and/or stability.
source: Together, these data indicate that the Cdc45–Psf1 interaction evident from the EM data plays a critical role in CMG formation and/or stability.
evidence: Mutagenesis data disrupting this interface prevents CMG formation, supporting this conclusion.

claim: The Mcm2-7 central channel and the Cdc45 DNA tracking groove are offset by approximately 90°.
source: In the DNA-bound model, the CMG still exhibits two channels; however, docking of the Cdc45 RecJ domain shows that its exonuclease/DNA-tracking groove is offset by 90° with respect to the central axis of the Mcm2-7 pore (Figure 3C).
evidence: Figure 3C shows the relative orientations of the Mcm2-7 channel and Cdc45 groove.

claim: If Cdc45 were to bind DNA in a manner similar to RecJ, it would be poised to capture the leading DNA strand that might escape from Mcm5-2 gate.
source: This orientation indicates that, were Cdc45 to bind DNA in a manner similar to RecJ, it would be poised to capture the leading DNA strand that might escape from Mcm5-2 gate (Figure 3D).
evidence: The structural orientation of Cdc45 relative to the Mcm2/5 gate supports this functional model.

claim: Cross-linking data show that Cdc45 engages the leading strand of a fork substrate only in the absence of nucleotide.
source: Consistent with this idea, cross-linking data in work to be published elsewhere (Petojevic et al.) show both that Cdc45 engages the leading strand of a fork substrate only in the absence of nucleotide
evidence: Reference to unpublished cross-linking data supports the DNA capture model.

claim: Cdc45-DNA interaction is ablated by mutation of residues suggested by the model to be important for DNA binding.
source: and that this interaction is ablated by the mutation of residues suggested by the model to be important for DNA binding.
evidence: Mutagenesis data from unpublished work validates the structural model.

claim: The AAA+ ATPase ring of Mcm2-7 is no longer flat in the DNA-bound state but adopts a clear right-handed spiral.
source: Notably, when comparing the new DNA-bound CMG model to the prior substrate-free state, we found that the AAA+ ATPase ring is no longer flat, but instead adopts a clear right-handed spiral (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Comparison of DNA-bound and apo structures shown in Figure 4A,B reveals this conformational change.

claim: The conformational change to a spiral does not propagate into the N-terminal domains, which maintain a roughly planar character.
source: This change in conformation does not propagate into the N-terminal domains, which maintain a roughly planar character (Figure 1E)
evidence: Figure 1E shows that the N-terminal domains remain planar despite C-terminal domain spiraling.

claim: The N-terminal domains form a relatively stable collar that likely helps to coordinate and restrain movements of the associated C-terminal ATPase regions.
source: The observed asymmetry between the two MCM tiers indicates that the N-terminal domains form a relatively stable collar that likely helps to coordinate and restrain movements of the associated C-terminal ATPase regions.
evidence: The differential behavior of N- and C-terminal domains supports this functional interpretation.

claim: The largest inter-subunit shifts within the Mcm2-7 ring occur between Mcm subunits 2 and 5.
source: First, the largest inter-subunit shifts within the Mcm2-7 ring, which occur between Mcm subunits 2 and 5, also correspond to the point where the GINS–Cdc45 complex docks against the helicase.
evidence: Structural analysis reveals the magnitude of shifts between different Mcm subunits.

claim: GINS–Cdc45 wedges itself between the N- and C-terminal tiers of the Mcm2-7 ring.
source: Inspection of the DNA-bound model reveals that GINS–Cdc45 does not simply straddle the Mcm2/5 interface, but that portions of the accessory subunits actually wedge themselves between the N- and C-terminal tiers of the Mcm2-7 ring (Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1D shows how GINS–Cdc45 inserts between MCM tiers.

claim: GINS–Cdc45 binding widens the exterior groove between the MCM N- and C-terminal domains at their points-of-contact.
source: This action widens the exterior groove between the MCM N- and C-terminal domains at their points-of-contact with GINS–Cdc45
evidence: Structural analysis shows the effect of GINS–Cdc45 wedging on MCM domain spacing.

claim: GINS–Cdc45 binding causes a concomitant narrowing of the groove on the exterior MCM face opposite the GINS–Cdc45 binding site (i.e., Mcm4).
source: and is offset by a concomitant narrowing of the groove on the exterior MCM face opposite the GINS–Cdc45 binding site (i.e., Mcm4, Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1D shows the compensatory narrowing at Mcm4.

claim: GINS–Cdc45 help stabilize a spiral configuration of ATPase centers when DNA is present.
source: The structural consequences resulting from GINS–Cdc45 binding suggests that these accessory subunits not only play a role in blocking access through the Mcm2/5 gate, as has been seen previously (Costa et al., 2011), but that they also help stabilize a spiral configuration of ATPase centers when DNA is present.
evidence: The wedging action of GINS–Cdc45 and its correlation with spiral formation supports this functional role.

claim: Mutation of active site residues at the Mcm2/5 interface ablates helicase activity.
source: Since the mutation of active site residues at the Mcm2/5 interface ablates helicase activity (Bochman et al., 2008; Ilves et al., 2010)
evidence: Citations to prior mutagenesis studies demonstrate the importance of the Mcm2/5 interface for activity.

claim: The spiral state observed in the structure inter-converts with another conformation in which the Mcm2/5 interface is remodeled to form a catalytically functional ATPase center during the translocation cycle.
source: it is likely that the spiral state observed here, which positionally offsets the ATP-binding site of Mcm5 from the arginine-finger residue of Mcm2, inter-converts with another conformation in which the Mcm2/5 interface is remodeled to form a catalytically functional ATPase center during the translocation cycle.
evidence: The structural offset of the Mcm2/5 active site in the spiral combined with the requirement for this interface for activity supports this model.

claim: The width of the Mcm2-7 central channel is approximately 30–35 Å.
source: The width of the Mcm2-7 central channel (as measured from homology models of the motor domains docked into the EM density) is likewise significantly larger (∼30–35 Å) compared to E1 (∼14 Å), and more closely approaches that of DnaB (∼22 Å).
evidence: Measurement from the structural model provides this dimension.

claim: The E1 helicase central channel is approximately 14 Å wide.
source: The width of the Mcm2-7 central channel (as measured from homology models of the motor domains docked into the EM density) is likewise significantly larger (∼30–35 Å) compared to E1 (∼14 Å)
evidence: Comparison with published E1 structure provides this dimension.

claim: The DnaB helicase central channel is approximately 22 Å wide.
source: and more closely approaches that of DnaB (∼22 Å).
evidence: Comparison with published DnaB structure provides this dimension.

claim: In E1 and DnaB, the difference in channel diameter and subunit rise sculpts the DNA substrate into a single-stranded helix whose relative pitches differ significantly.
source: Interestingly, in E1 and DnaB the difference in channel diameter and subunit rise between the two proteins sculpts the DNA substrate bound by each helicase into a single-stranded helix whose relative pitches differ significantly
evidence: Comparison of E1 and DnaB structures reveals this relationship between channel geometry and DNA conformation.

claim: Each subunit of DnaB engages two nucleotides of DNA.
source: these geometric differences allow each subunit of DnaB to engage two nucleotides of DNA (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012)
evidence: Citation to prior structural work on DnaB-DNA complex.

claim: E1 binds only a single nucleotide per protomer.
source: whereas E1 binds only a single nucleotide per protomer (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006).
evidence: Citation to prior structural work on E1-DNA complex.

claim: The similarity of the Mcm2-7 spiral to DnaB raises the possibility that the helicase might translocate with a step-size greater than one nucleotide per ATP consumed.
source: The similarity of the Mcm2-7 spiral to DnaB raises the interesting possibility that the helicase might translocate with a step-size greater than one nucleotide per ATP consumed
evidence: The structural similarity to DnaB, which binds two nucleotides per subunit, suggests this possibility.

claim: The MCM N-terminal DNA-binding collar of Pyrococcus furiosus binds four nucleotides per subunit.
source: consistent with this notion, a recent study has shown that the MCM N-terminal DNA-binding collar of Pyrococcus furiosus binds four nucleotides per subunit (Froelich et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to recent work on archaeal MCM DNA binding supports the multi-nucleotide step-size model.

claim: The proteasome base contains six homologous AAA+ ATPase subunits (Rpt1-6).
source: The proteasome consists of several discrete subcomplexes including a heterohexameric unfoldase region, termed the 'base', which (like the CMG) contains six homologous AAA+ ATPase subunits (Rpt1-6) (Forster et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation to prior work on proteasome structure.

claim: Cryo-EM studies have imaged the complete 26S yeast proteasome bound to ATP at approximately 9 Å resolution showing that the AAA+ subunits of the base form a right-handed spiral.
source: Recent cryo-EM studies have imaged the complete 26S yeast proteasome bound to ATP at ∼9 Å resolution showing that the AAA+ subunits of the base also form a right-handed spiral (Lander et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation to prior cryo-EM work on proteasome structure.

claim: The proteasome spiral and the CMG spiral exhibit a surprisingly similar global architecture.
source: Comparison of proteasome spiral with that seen here for the CMG shows that these regions of the two systems exhibit a surprisingly similar global architecture (Figure 4E).
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 4E reveals this similarity.

claim: The proteasome accessory subunit Rpn1 wedges itself between a subset of ATPase and OB-fold domains present in Rpt1-6.
source: Moreover, the proteasome also contains an accessory subunit (Rpn1) that—as observed here for GINS–Cdc45 in the context of the CMG—wedges itself between a subset of ATPase and OB-fold domains present in Rpt1-6 (Lander et al., 2012; Figure 4E).
evidence: Citation to prior proteasome structure and comparison shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The CMG and proteasome ATPase subcomplexes may share commonalities in how ATP turnover is coupled to movements that promote translocation.
source: The structural congruencies exhibited between the CMG and proteasome ATPase subcomplexes suggest that, even though the substrates for the two systems differ greatly, both motors may share certain commonalities in how ATP turnover is coupled to movements that promote translocation.
evidence: The structural similarities between CMG and proteasome support this speculation about shared mechanisms.

claim: Both the CMG and proteasome show relatively high degrees of tolerance toward active-site mutations within certain subunits.
source: Such a similarity could underlie both the pronounced asymmetry of the CMG and proteasome ATPase rings, and the relatively high degree of tolerance shown by both systems toward active-site mutations within certain subunits (Moreau et al., 2007; Ilves et al., 2010; Beckwith et al., 2013).
evidence: Citations to prior mutagenesis studies on both systems support this observation.

claim: The CMG has been observed to operate as a discrete single complex during replication.
source: Although the CMG has been observed to operate as a discrete single complex during replication (Yardimci et al., 2010)
evidence: Citation to prior work on CMG function during replication.

claim: The loading of Mcm2-7 hexamer onto DNA by ORC, Cdc6, and Cdt1 during initiation results in the transient formation of a catalytically inactive, head-to-head double hexamer intermediate.
source: the loading of the Mcm2-7 hexamer onto DNA by ORC, Cdc6, and Cdt1 during initiation results in the transient formation of a catalytically inactive, head-to-head double hexamer intermediate (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009).
evidence: Citations to prior work on Mcm2-7 loading and double hexamer formation.

claim: The MCM N-terminal domains comprise the dimer interface of the double hexamer.
source: The MCM N-terminal domains have been shown to comprise the dimer interface of the double hexamer (Fletcher et al., 2003; Costa et al., 2006; Remus et al., 2009)
evidence: Citations to prior structural and biochemical work on MCM double hexamer interface.

claim: The MCM N-terminal domains create a critical target site for the Dbf4-dependent Cdc7 protein kinase DDK.
source: and create a critical target site for the Dbf4-dependent Cdc7 protein kinase DDK (Labib, 2010; Sheu and Stillman, 2006, 2010)
evidence: Citations to prior work on DDK phosphorylation targets.

claim: Phosphorylation of the N-terminal tails of Mcm2/4/6 alters the configuration of the Mcm2-7 complex but does not directly promote Mcm2-7 dissociation.
source: phosphorylation of the N-terminal tails of Mcm2/4/6 alters the configuration of the Mcm2-7 complex, but does not directly promote Mcm2-7 dissociation (On et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to recent work on the effects of DDK phosphorylation.

claim: A small (approximately 5%) but consistent population of CMG particles forms a clear dimeric species that adopts a distinctive head-to-head configuration through its MCM N-terminal regions.
source: In particular, a small (∼5%) but consistent population of CMG particles was seen to form a clear dimeric species that adopts a distinctive head-to-head configuration through its MCM N-terminal regions, and which consistently orients the GINS–Cdc45 subcomplex toward opposing sides of the two ring (Figure 5A).
evidence: EM data shown in Figure 5A reveals this dimeric population.

claim: The dimeric CMG consistently orients the GINS–Cdc45 subcomplex toward opposing sides of the two rings.
source: a small (∼5%) but consistent population of CMG particles was seen to form a clear dimeric species that adopts a distinctive head-to-head configuration through its MCM N-terminal regions, and which consistently orients the GINS–Cdc45 subcomplex toward opposing sides of the two ring (Figure 5A).
evidence: EM class averages shown in Figure 5A demonstrate this consistent orientation.

claim: The abundance and uniformity of CMG dimers suggests that these particles represent a naturally occurring state of the assembly.
source: The abundance and uniformity of CMG dimers, which were noted in several independent preparations, suggests that these particles represent a naturally occurring state of the assembly.
evidence: The consistent observation of dimers across multiple preparations supports this interpretation.

claim: The 180° offset of GINS and Cdc45 in the dimer places each Mcm2/5 gate on opposite sides of the complex, facing away from each other.
source: For example, the 180° offset of GINS and Cdc45 present in the dimer places each Mcm2/5 gate on the opposite sides of the complex, facing away from each other (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Analysis of the dimer structure shown in Figure 5B,C reveals this arrangement.

claim: During origin melting, the configuration of the CMG dimer would allow a single DNA strand to escape each Mcm2-7 hexamer without steric interference from its partner CMG, enabling particle separation and the formation of two independent replication forks.
source: During origin melting, this configuration would allow a single DNA strand to escape each Mcm2-7 hexamer without steric interference from its partner CMG, enabling particle separation and the formation of two independent replication forks.
evidence: The structural arrangement of gates in the dimer supports this functional model.

claim: The N-terminal regions of Mcm2 and Mcm5 of one hexamer associate in trans with the N-terminal regions of Mcm6 and Mcm4 of the partner hexamer.
source: The organization of the CMG dimer also indicates that the N-terminal regions of Mcm2 and Mcm5 of one hexamer associate in trans with the N-terminal regions of Mcm6 and Mcm4 of the partner hexamer.
evidence: Analysis of the dimer structure and comparison with computational models reveals this subunit register.

claim: Mcm4 and GINS have been seen to interact in pulldown studies.
source: Such an interaction would help explain why Mcm4 and GINS have been seen to interact in pulldown studies (Ilves et al., 2010)
evidence: Citation to prior biochemical interaction studies.

claim: Mcm4 and GINS map to distal positions of the CMG in the context of a monomer.
source: even though the two factors map to distal positions of the CMG in the context of a monomer (Costa et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to prior structural work on monomeric CMG.

claim: The ability of DDK to activate Mcm2-7 by phosphorylation of Mcm4, 2, and 6 could result from a destabilization of the CMG dimer contacts that are symmetrically apposed across the N-terminal collar.
source: Finally, the observed arrangement suggests that the ability of DDK to activate Mcm2-7 by phosphorylation of Mcm4, 2, and 6 (Labib, 2010) (as well as the ability of the Bob1 mutation in Mcm5 to bypass the requirement for DDK [Jackson et al., 1993]) could result from a destabilization of the CMG dimer contacts that are symmetrically apposed across the N-terminal collar (Figure 5C).
evidence: The structural arrangement of DDK target sites in the dimer interface supports this mechanistic model.

claim: The Bob1 mutation in Mcm5 can bypass the requirement for DDK.
source: (as well as the ability of the Bob1 mutation in Mcm5 to bypass the requirement for DDK [Jackson et al., 1993])
evidence: Citation to prior genetic work on DDK bypass mutations.

claim: The two Mcm2/5 gates of a double hexamer are spatially segregated from each other.
source: Altogether, our data establish that the two Mcm2/5 gates of a double hexamer are spatially segregated from each other
evidence: The dimer structure directly shows the spatial separation of the two gates.

claim: Separation of Mcm2-7 double hexamers occurs subsequent to CMG formation.
source: and indicate that separation of Mcm2-7 double hexamers occurs subsequent to CMG formation.
evidence: The observation of CMG dimers indicates that CMG formation precedes double hexamer separation.

claim: Phosphorylation by DDK is insufficient to promote the separation of Mcm2-7 double hexamers on its own.
source: Such a mechanism is consistent with recent findings showing that the phosphorylation by DDK is insufficient to promote the separation of Mcm2-7 double hexamers on its own (On et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to recent work on DDK function supports this conclusion.

claim: Mcm2-7 on its own possesses a natural discontinuity—the 'Mcm2/5 gate'—through which DNA can enter and exit the helicase pore.
source: Biochemical studies using Saccharomyces cerevisiae proteins first showed that Mcm2-7 on its own possesses a natural discontinuity—the 'Mcm2/5 gate'—through which DNA can enter and exit the helicase pore (Bochman and Schwacha, 2007).
evidence: Citation to prior biochemical work on the Mcm2/5 gate.

claim: Metazoan Mcm2-7 rings preferentially assume a left-handed lock-washer shape.
source: Structural studies have corroborated this observation, additionally showing that metazoan Mcm2-7 rings preferentially assume a left-handed lock-washer shape and that ATP alone is incapable of fully inducing ring closure (Costa et al., 2011; Lyubimov et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations to prior structural work on Mcm2-7 conformation.

claim: ATP alone is incapable of fully inducing ring closure in metazoan Mcm2-7.
source: Structural studies have corroborated this observation, additionally showing that metazoan Mcm2-7 rings preferentially assume a left-handed lock-washer shape and that ATP alone is incapable of fully inducing ring closure (Costa et al., 2011; Lyubimov et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations to prior structural work on Mcm2-7 nucleotide-dependent conformations.

claim: Following the action of ORC, Cdc6, and Cdt1, two Mcm2-7 hexamers become locked into a planarized co-joined ring.
source: Following the action of ORC, Cdc6, and Cdt1, two Mcm2-7 hexamers become locked into a planarized co-joined ring (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009)
evidence: Citations to prior work on Mcm2-7 loading and double hexamer formation.

claim: In the presence of GINS, Cdc45, and single-stranded DNA, the Mcm2-7 ATPase domains shift into a right-handed spiral conformation.
source: in the presence of GINS, Cdc45, and single-stranded DNA, the Mcm2-7 ATPase domains shift again, but now into a right-handed spiral conformation (Figure 4).
evidence: The current structural data shown in Figure 4 demonstrates this conformation.

claim: Mcm2-7 undergoes a chiral-flip in architectural state as it matures into a functional helicase.
source: Thus, Mcm2-7 undergoes a chiral-flip in architectural state as it matures into a functional helicase with loading, activation, and DNA binding all appearing to participate in these transitions.
evidence: Comparison of left-handed apo state with right-handed DNA-bound state reveals this chiral transition.

claim: The isolated metazoan Mcm2-7 motor forms an inactive left-handed spiral, irrespective of nucleotide state, with a discontinuity between Mcm5 and Mcm2.
source: Following synthesis and assembly, the isolated metazoan Mcm2-7 motor forms an inactive left-handed spiral, irrespective of nucleotide state, with a discontinuity between Mcm5 and Mcm2.
evidence: This summarizes prior structural findings on apo Mcm2-7.

claim: Dpb11-Sld2-Sld3 chaperone GINS and Cdc45 onto the Mcm2-7 double hexamer.
source: Following loading, Dpb11-Sld2-Sld3 (11-2-3) chaperone GINS and Cdc45 onto the Mcm2-7 double hexamer
evidence: This describes the known pathway for CMG assembly based on prior work.

claim: DDK-promoted phosphorylation events help promote both DNA melting, CMG formation and replication fork separation.
source: and along with DDK promoted phosphorylation events, help promote both DNA melting, CMG formation and replication fork separation.
evidence: This summarizes the known roles of DDK in replication initiation based on prior work.

claim: Structural analysis of dimeric CMG particles indicates that the Mcm2/5 gates are localized on the opposing sides of the dodecameric Mcm2-7 complex.
source: Structural analysis of dimeric CMG particles (Figure 5) indicates that the Mcm2/5 gates are localized on the opposing sides of the dodecameric Mcm2-7 complex
evidence: Analysis of the dimer structure shown in Figure 5 reveals this arrangement.

claim: CMG formation precedes separation of the double hexamer.
source: and that CMG formation precedes separation of the double hexamer.
evidence: The observation of CMG dimers supports this temporal ordering of events.

claim: Mcm2-7 might initially assemble into an inactive conformation to prevent inadvertently triggering aberrant replication events.
source: One possibility is that Mcm2-7 initially assembles into an inactive conformation to prevent inadvertently triggering aberrant replication events.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why Mcm2-7 adopts different conformational states.

claim: Mcm2-7 might transition through different forms as a means to promote the melting of duplex replication origins.
source: An alternative possibility, not necessarily incompatible with the first, is that Mcm2-7 might transition through different forms as a means to promote the melting of duplex replication origins.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the functional significance of conformational transitions.

claim: Two MCM-associated factors—Cdt1 and GINS–Cdc45—both appear to occlude the Mcm2/5 interface.
source: Given the topological barrier that extended DNA segments present to encirclement by toroidal proteins, it is notable that two MCM-associated factors—Cdt1 and GINS–Cdc45—both appear to occlude the Mcm2/5 interface (Costa et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: Citations to prior structural work showing how these factors interact with the Mcm2/5 gate.

claim: Controlled access through the Mcm2/5 gate is useful for regulating DNA access into a preformed Mcm2-7 hexamer.
source: Hence, controlled access through the Mcm2/5 gate appears useful not only for regulating DNA access into a preformed Mcm2-7 hexamer (Bochman and Schwacha, 2007)
evidence: Citation to prior work on gate function combined with structural observations.

claim: Controlled access through the Mcm2/5 gate is useful for preventing accidental DNA egress in the apo state and at stalled forks.
source: but also for preventing accidental DNA egress in the apo state and at stalled forks (Petojevic et al., unpublished data).
evidence: Reference to unpublished data supports this additional function of gate control.

claim: The CMG complex did not behave well during cryo-preservation attempts using holey-carbon EM grids.
source: The complex did not behave well during cryo-preservation attempts using holey-carbon EM grids, so samples were instead deposited onto continuous carbon grids and exposed to uranyl formate for negative staining.
evidence: This describes a technical challenge encountered during sample preparation.

claim: Images were acquired with JADAS automated data collection software on a JEM2100 electron microscope.
source: A total of 29,913 particles were selected from EM micrographs acquired with JADAS automated data collection software (JEOL, Zhang et al., 2009) on a JEM2100 electron microscope.
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology.

claim: A 3D model was generated by projection matching using a low-pass filtered (60 Å), free-hand test-validated, nucleotide-bound structure of the CMG as a starting model.
source: Following particle picking and 2D averaging, a 3D model was generated by projection matching using a low-pass filtered (60 Å), free-hand test-validated, nucleotide-bound structure of the CMG as a starting model ('Materials and methods'; Rosenthal and Henderson, 2003; Lyubimov et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the 3D reconstruction methodology and starting model validation.
